stops.narrative: Distinguish objects found together in a wreck from a fully reconstructed route.
Separate a tree-ring drought finding, political transformation and the changing occupation of a capital.
Inspect a Kerma vessel excavated in Egypt. Keep the pot’s context separate from the proposed origin of a person.
Explore ritual writing and skilled casting without imposing Anatolia’s chronology on China.
Inspect a small ceramic figure and think about how its scale differs from communal monuments.
Ask how dated patterns, settlements and food remains can support different accounts of voyaging.

conclusion: A network can be demonstrated without knowing every route. A political center can change without all its people vanishing. A dated drought can matter without explaining everything. Elsewhere, other communities faced their own histories and choices.

evidence.prompt: What can the Hittite drought study support?

options.text: A severe environmental stress occurred near the political transformation; direct causation remains unproved.
options.feedback: The authors explicitly preserve that distinction. Other political, social and regional evidence still matters.

options.text: Exactly the same disaster ended every society in the world in 1200 BCE.
options.feedback: The evidence is regional, and other societies had different chronologies. A shared date on an atlas creates no shared cause.

options.text: Every place at Hattusha was occupied and destroyed simultaneously.
options.feedback: The archaeological abstract emphasizes changing areas of occupation and warns against treating the combined plan as one moment.
